newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Santer says stable euro will help create jobs.
newsitem.headline: Santer says stable euro will help create jobs.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer said on Thursday there was no turning back on the road to a single European currency and held out the hope that closer economic ties would stem rising joblessness.

"We can say with the greatest amount of confidence that the (single currency) project has become irreversible and that the euro will see the light of day on January 1, 1999," Santer told a one-day European economic forum in Vienna.
He said that a single currency born of sound budgetary policies would deliver low inflation and interest rates while boosting investment, growth and jobs.

But he warned that the benefits of the euro would depend on the ability of EU members to maintain fiscal discipline beyond 1997, when the starting group for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be chosen.
"It is important that member states do not consider the year 1997 to be a special year after which they can let their deficits slip again," Santer said.

He threw his weight behind German proposals for a stability pact for countries joining the single currency. Germany has demanded tough rules to penalise governments that run excessive deficits within a monetary union.
"The Commission wholeheartedly supports the idea of a stability pact presented by German Finance Minister (Theo) Waigel," he said.
Santer won backing from Austrian National Bank president Klaus Liebscher and Chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
"The planned stability pact is extremely important...We hope for early and concrete results. A credible stability pact would send a very positive signal to financial markets," Liebscher said.
Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen encouraged the 15-member bloc to establish an exchange rate mechanism that would avoid rifts between participating and non-participating nations.
Danes voted in a 1993 referendum to endorse the Maastricht Treaty on condition that Denmark did not join EMU.
"EMU is not only a question for the 'ins', it is also a question for the 'outs'," he told a news conference.
Rasmussen reinforced Denmark's commitment to economic convergence within the EU and joined Santer and Vranitzky in calling for more action to fight rising unemployment.
Santer said joblessness wasted human resources, put enormous strains on the social security system and ultimately posed a social threat.

A single currency, based on sound economic policies, would create an environment conducive to job creation and investment. His long-standing proposal for a "confidence pact" to tackle joblessness went one step further, Santer said.
"The main economic objective for the European Union is to combat the unacceptably high rates of unemployment that are undermining our society," he said.
